The paper investigates the theory of Hardy-Lorentz spaces \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\), where \(0<p\leq 1\) and \(0<q\leq \infty\). These spaces combine features of classical Hardy spaces and Lorentz spaces, making them useful in the study of functions and distributions whose behavior is too singular to be treated within the usual \(L^p\) framework. Since the range \(0<p\leq 1\) lies outside the Banach space setting, the analysis requires refined tools from harmonic analysis, particularly those related to maximal functions, distributions, and quasi-normed spaces.

A central topic of the paper is the atomic decomposition of elements in Hardy-Lorentz spaces. Atomic decompositions provide a way to represent functions or distributions as sums of simpler building blocks called atoms. These atoms are typically supported on cubes or balls, satisfy size conditions, and have certain cancellation properties expressed through vanishing moments. By decomposing an element of \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) into such atoms, one obtains a concrete and flexible description of the space. This representation is especially important because it allows problems about general elements of Hardy-Lorentz spaces to be reduced to estimates on atoms, which are much easier to handle.

The paper also examines interpolation properties of Hardy-Lorentz spaces. Interpolation theory studies how spaces and operators behave between two given endpoint spaces. In this context, the authors consider how Hardy-Lorentz spaces fit into interpolation scales and how one may recover intermediate Hardy-Lorentz spaces from suitable pairs of Hardy-type spaces. These results clarify the structural relationship between different choices of the parameters \(p\) and \(q\), and they are useful for proving boundedness results for operators. In particular, interpolation provides a powerful method for extending estimates known on certain endpoint spaces to a broader family of Hardy-Lorentz spaces.

Another major focus is the behavior of singular integral operators and related operators acting on Hardy-Lorentz spaces. Singular integrals play a fundamental role in harmonic analysis and partial differential equations, but their boundedness on spaces with low integrability and quasi-Banach structure can be delicate. The paper analyzes conditions under which such operators are bounded from one Hardy-Lorentz space into another, or from a Hardy-Lorentz space into a Lorentz or weak-type space. The atomic decomposition results are especially useful here, since boundedness can often be verified by checking how an operator acts on individual atoms and then summing the resulting estimates appropriately.

Overall, the paper develops foundational aspects of Hardy-Lorentz spaces \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) in the range \(0<p\leq 1\). By establishing atomic decompositions, studying interpolation, and analyzing the action of singular integrals and other operators, it provides a framework for extending classical Hardy space techniques to the finer Lorentz scale. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of function spaces that arise naturally in harmonic analysis and offer tools for applications to operator theory and related areas.

This paper investigates the Hardy-Lorentz spaces \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\), where \(0<p\le 1\) and \(0<q\le \infty\). These spaces refine the classical Hardy spaces by replacing the usual \(L^p\) scale with the more delicate Lorentz scale \(L^{p,q}\). As a result, they provide a flexible framework for studying functions and distributions whose size and integrability properties cannot be fully captured by ordinary Hardy spaces alone. The main goal of the paper is to develop a systematic theory for \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) and to examine how important operators from harmonic analysis behave on these spaces.

A central part of the study is the atomic decomposition of Hardy-Lorentz spaces. The paper shows that elements of \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) can be represented as sums of suitable atoms, where the atoms satisfy size, support, and moment cancellation conditions. This decomposition gives a concrete description of the elements of the space and makes it possible to reduce many problems to estimates on individual atoms. Such atomic characterizations are especially important in the range \(0<p\le1\), where the spaces are no longer Banach spaces in general and standard methods based on convexity are often unavailable.

The paper also uses interpolation theory to relate Hardy-Lorentz spaces to one another and to connect them with other function spaces in harmonic analysis. Interpolation provides a powerful method for deriving boundedness results and structural properties from known endpoint estimates. Through this approach, the paper clarifies how the Lorentz parameter \(q\) influences the behavior of the spaces and how \(H^{p,q}\) fits naturally between different Hardy-type scales.

Another major focus is the boundedness of operators on \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\). The paper studies singular integral operators and related linear or sublinear operators, giving conditions under which they extend boundedly from Hardy-Lorentz spaces into appropriate target spaces. In particular, the atomic decomposition allows the analysis of such operators to be reduced to uniform estimates on atoms, together with suitable control away from their supports. This method is used to establish boundedness results for classical operators arising in Calderón-Zygmund theory and related areas.

Overall, the paper provides a detailed account of the structure of Hardy-Lorentz spaces and their role in harmonic analysis. By combining atomic methods, interpolation techniques, and operator estimates, it establishes a coherent framework for understanding \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) in the critical range \(0<p\le1\). The results clarify the relationship between Hardy spaces, Lorentz spaces, and singular integral theory, and they show how operators that are well understood on classical Hardy or Lebesgue spaces can be extended to this more refined setting.

Hardy and Lorentz are two important names in mathematical analysis, especially in the study of function spaces and inequalities.

The term **Hardy** often refers to the work of G. H. Hardy, whose contributions include the famous **Hardy inequalities** and the theory of **Hardy spaces**. Hardy spaces are function spaces that play a central role in complex analysis, harmonic analysis, and partial differential equations. They are useful for studying boundary behavior of analytic functions and for understanding how functions can be decomposed and estimated.

**Lorentz spaces**, named after George Lorentz, are refinements of the classical Lebesgue spaces. While Lebesgue spaces measure the integrability of a function using a single exponent, Lorentz spaces provide a more precise scale by taking into account the distribution of the size of a function. This makes them especially useful in interpolation theory, harmonic analysis, and the study of sharp forms of inequalities.

Together, **Hardy and Lorentz spaces** appear in many advanced areas of analysis. For example, Hardy-type inequalities can be studied within Lorentz spaces to obtain sharper estimates than those available in ordinary Lebesgue spaces. These ideas are important in the analysis of singular integral operators, Sobolev embeddings, and regularity theory for partial differential equations.

In short, Hardy’s work provides fundamental tools for estimating functions and operators, while Lorentz spaces offer a refined framework for measuring function size. The combination of Hardy and Lorentz ideas gives mathematicians powerful methods for dealing with delicate problems in modern analysis.

counterfactuals.output:
The spaces \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\), often understood as Hardy–amalgam spaces, provide a two-parameter refinement of classical real Hardy spaces \(H^p\) and Wiener amalgam spaces. They measure local Hardy-type behavior with exponent \(p\) together with global amalgam summability governed by \(q\). Such spaces are particularly useful when one wants to distinguish local singular behavior from global decay or distribution.

A central result is the atomic characterization of \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\). For suitable ranges of \(0<p\leq 1\) and \(0<q\leq \infty\), every element of \(H^{p,q}\) can be decomposed into a sum of atoms supported on cubes, satisfying size and moment cancellation conditions. Typically, an atom \(a\) is supported in a cube \(Q\), obeys a norm bound such as  
\[
\|a\|_{L^r}\leq |Q|^{1/r-1/p},
\]
for an appropriate \(r>1\), and has vanishing moments up to a prescribed order depending on \(p\) and \(n\). The corresponding coefficient sequence is controlled in an amalgam-type quasi-norm. Conversely, any such atomic expansion defines an element of \(H^{p,q}\). This extends the classical Coifman–Weiss atomic theory for \(H^p\).

Interpolation results show that the scale \(H^{p,q}\) behaves well under both real and complex interpolation. In appropriate parameter ranges, interpolating between two Hardy–amalgam spaces yields another space of the same type, with interpolated indices:
\[
(H^{p_0,q_0},H^{p_1,q_1})_\theta
   \simeq H^{p_\theta,q_\theta},
\]
where
\[
\frac1{p_\theta}=\frac{1-\theta}{p_0}+\frac{\theta}{p_1},
\qquad
\frac1{q_\theta}=\frac{1-\theta}{q_0}+\frac{\theta}{q_1}.
\]
Such results connect the Hardy–amalgam scale to Lorentz, Lebesgue, and classical Hardy spaces, and are important for transferring boundedness theorems.

Singular integral operators also admit boundedness results on \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\). Calderón–Zygmund operators with sufficient smoothness and cancellation extend boundedly from \(H^{p,q}\) into itself, or into suitable amalgam or Lebesgue-type target spaces, depending on the indices. The proof typically combines atomic decompositions with kernel estimates: one controls the operator near the support of each atom using \(L^r\)-boundedness and away from the support using cancellation and smoothness of the kernel. These arguments parallel the classical Hardy-space theory but require additional bookkeeping for the global \(q\)-summability.

Overall, the theory of \(H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\) unifies local Hardy-space phenomena, atomic methods, interpolation theory, and Calderón–Zygmund analysis. It extends many fundamental results from \(H^p\) to a broader framework capable of capturing both local regularity and global distribution of functions or distributions.
